analysis.one_liner: Criminalizes knowingly selling counterfeit prescription drugs and gives the FDA mandatory recall authority.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: after introduction it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee's Health Subcommittee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Named for a teenager who was injected with a counterfeit drug during transplant surgery, the bill would make it a crime punishable by any term of years, or life, to knowingly sell prescription drugs that have been adulterated, misbranded, or passed off as approved drugs. It would require drug makers to alert federal regulators within 48 hours of learning a counterfeit may have entered the supply, require anti-counterfeiting technology in manufacturing, tighten rules tracking who has handled a drug as it moves from maker to pharmacy, and for the first time give the Secretary of Health and Human Services mandatory authority to order a dangerous drug off the market and recall it. It would also add $60 million a year for FDA inspections and $5 million a year for public education.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients filling prescriptions, especially those getting injectable or high-cost drugs, gain protection against counterfeit drugs reaching them through the supply chain. Legitimate manufacturers also gain, since counterfeit versions compete with their products, though they take on new reporting, tracking, and recall obligations in exchange.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime, punishable by any term of years up to life plus fines, to knowingly cause a prescription drug to be adulterated, misbranded, or misrepresented as an approved drug and sell or trade it — or to knowingly buy or trade for such a drug.
Requires drug manufacturers to notify the Secretary of Health and Human Services within 48 hours after learning information that reasonably suggests a counterfeit-related violation may have occurred.

Gives the Secretary mandatory authority, upon finding a reasonable probability that a drug would cause serious adverse health consequences or death, to order an immediate stop to its distribution and, after an informal hearing, to require a recall.

Authorizes $60 million per year for fiscal years 2010 through 2014 in added FDA funding for inspections, examinations, and investigations of counterfeit-drug violations, plus $5 million per year for public and clinician education about counterfeit drugs.

Strips exemptions for 'authorized distributors of record' from the drug pedigree rules, and directs the Secretary to set requirements for identifying the chain of custody of a drug from the manufacturer to the dispensing pharmacy, with equivalent certainty.
Authorizes the FDA Chief Counsel to issue subpoenas in investigations of acts that may threaten the public health.

analysis.who_pays: Drug manufacturers take on new compliance costs: 48-hour reporting of suspected counterfeits, possible mandatory anti-counterfeiting technology in manufacturing, publicly available lists of authorized distributors, and exposure to mandatory cease-distribution and recall orders. Drug wholesalers and distributors face tightened chain-of-custody record requirements. The Treasury funds the new FDA inspection and education spending. Persons convicted under the new criminal provisions face prison terms up to life.

drawbacks.text: The bill would deem a drug misbranded if it is not manufactured using anti-counterfeiting technologies the Secretary determines are technically feasible, a broad standard that would impose compliance costs on manufacturers without Congress first specifying what the technology must be.

A cease-distribution order could shut down a drug's supply immediately, with only an informal hearing guaranteed within 10 days afterward, giving companies facing the order limited process while the order stands.

The criminal penalties run up to any term of years or life imprisonment, which some would argue is disproportionate for commercial conduct, even knowing counterfeiting, compared with other federal offenses.
The bill authorizes $65 million in new annual federal spending ($60 million for FDA enforcement plus $5 million for education) for five fiscal years, an added cost to taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections are targeted and would likely prevent deaths like the one that gave the bill its name: criminal penalties aimed at knowing counterfeiters, faster manufacturer reporting, and mandatory federal recall authority that the FDA did not have for drugs at the time. The compliance costs fall on an industry that is also a beneficiary, since counterfeit goods undercut legitimate manufacturers, so the trade-off is modest for them and the main real cost is $65 million a year in appropriations. The vaguely defined technology mandate and the 10-day informal-hearing process for recall orders are the weakest design elements.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Health Subcommittee, and died there without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Israel introduced the bill on June 4, 2009, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On June 8, 2009, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where no further action was taken.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor, a single House Democrat, and never advanced beyond subcommittee referral before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and drug wholesalers are better off because the bill died: they faced no new 48-hour reporting duties, anti-counterfeiting technology mandates, tightened pedigree requirements, or mandatory recall authority. Counterfeiters also faced no added federal penalty. Patients were left with the pre-existing system, in which the FDA had to negotiate voluntary drug recalls rather than order them.

for.name: Rep. Steve Israel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 4, 2009, naming it for Tim Fagan, a constituent who received a counterfeit drug during transplant surgery.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on June 4, 2009, and never took it up for a markup or reported it out.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 8, 2009, and held no hearing or markup on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never came to a vote, and with a Democratic sponsor plus one Democratic cosponsor there is no record showing how the parties would have split.

industries.note: Counterfeit versions of their products undercut legitimate sales and endanger patients, so stronger enforcement and track-and-trace rules protect their revenue alongside patient safety; but the bill also imposes 48-hour reporting duties, possible mandatory anti-counterfeiting technology, public distributor lists, and mandatory cease-distribution and recall orders on them. At the time, the FDA had no mandatory recall authority over drugs, so this would have been a real new regulatory power.

The bill strips the pedigree-rule exemptions for authorized distributors of record and requires manufacturers to keep and publish lists of authorized distributors, squeezing out or burdening secondary wholesalers by tightening the documented chain of custody from maker to pharmacy. That burden is the mechanism that makes it harder for counterfeit drugs to slip into the supply chain, which protects patients.

The bill would have added $60 million a year for inspections and investigations and given the agency subpoena power and mandatory recall authority, expanding its capacity to police the drug supply on behalf of patients.
